title: Murph: History, Strategy, and Ways to Scale It

toc.title: Strategy: How to Partition the Reps
Pacing the Runs and the Vest

bodyHtml:
Who Murph Was

Every Memorial Day, gyms and garages across the country fill up with people about to take on the same brutal workout: a mile run, 100 pull-ups, 200 push-ups, 300 squats, then another mile run, often with a 20-pound vest. Most of them know it's a hero WOD. Fewer know the name behind it.

Michael Murphy was a Navy SEAL lieutenant killed in Afghanistan in June 2005 during Operation Red Wings, an action that later earned him the Medal of Honor for staying exposed under fire to call in support for his team. This was one of his own training routines before he died, and it was added to the hero WOD list that same year. The vest represents body armor. The format was his own conditioning test, not something built afterward just to be hard for the sake of hard.

That history matters because Murph gets treated like a stunt online: people filming themselves grinding through it in under 40 minutes, or arguing about whether cluster sets count as "real" Murph. The workout deserves better than that. It's worth doing seriously, and it's worth doing at a pace you can actually sustain, because that's closer to what it was built for in the first place.

What the Workout Actually Demands

On paper Murph looks simple: two 1-mile runs bookending 100 pull-ups, 200 push-ups, and 300 squats. In practice it's one of the longest continuous grinds in benchmark training, somewhere between 35 and 75 minutes depending on your conditioning and how you break up the middle.

The runs are rarely the problem. What wrecks people is going out too hot on the pull-ups and push-ups, then discovering 150 squats later that the legs that carried them through mile one are gone. Grip failure is the other quiet killer: pull-up sets that felt fine at rep 20 turn into one rep at a time by rep 70, and there's no shortcut around that except pacing from the start.

"Murph rewards the athlete who starts conservative more than the athlete who starts strong."

Strategy: How to Partition the Reps

Unbroken Murph, meaning 100 straight pull-ups, then 200 straight push-ups, then 300 straight squats, is almost never the fastest way to finish, and it's rarely the smartest way either. Most experienced athletes break the middle into rounds, commonly 20 rounds of 5 pull-ups, 10 push-ups, and 15 squats, which keeps heart rate manageable and lets you hold a pace for the full 20 rounds instead of blowing up halfway through.

Smaller partitions, like 10 rounds of 10 pull-ups, 20 push-ups, 30 squats, work well for athletes who move fast in bigger sets but still need occasional grip breaks. Bigger partitions, like 5 rounds of 20/40/60, suit athletes with a strong pull-up base who don't want the extra transition time. There isn't one right answer here. The right partition is whichever one keeps you moving instead of standing around deciding what to do next.

Practical habit: Test your partitioning scheme on a normal training day before you run it for real. Five rounds of a proposed rep scheme will tell you fast whether it's sustainable for twenty.

Pacing the Runs and the Vest

Treat the opening mile as a warm-up, not a time trial. Going out at 5K pace burns matches you'll want later at the pull-up bar. A controlled, conversational pace on mile one, then whatever you have left on mile two, produces better overall times for most people than trying to bank speed early.

The vest is where most scaling decisions actually belong. Twenty pounds changes push-up mechanics and squat depth more than people expect, and it turns the runs into something closer to a loaded ruck. Wearing it for the runs but stripping it for the strength portion is a common, completely legitimate variation. There's no rule that says it has to be all or nothing.

Ways to Scale It Honestly

Scaling Murph isn't a consolation prize. It's how most people should approach it the first several times through. A few honest options:

  • Half Murph: half-mile runs, 50/100/150 reps. Keeps the format and structure intact at roughly half the volume, a smart entry point for anyone new to hero WODs.
  • No vest: drop the weight and keep the reps as written. This is the standard scaling move, and nobody should feel bad about choosing it.
  • Ring rows instead of pull-ups: if strict or kipping pull-ups aren't there yet, ring rows keep the pulling stimulus without turning the workout into 100 failed attempts at the bar.
  • Knee push-ups or an elevated surface: same logic. Keep the movement pattern honest instead of grinding through reps that don't hit full range of motion.
  • Rowing or biking instead of running: useful if you're training somewhere without safe outdoor space, or coming back from an injury that limits impact.

The goal of any scale is the same: finish the workout at an intensity that still challenges you, using movements you can perform correctly the whole way through. That's a better benchmark than a fast number built on reps that came up short.

Final Thoughts

Murph shows up once a year for most people, and that's part of what makes it worth doing well. Walk in with a pacing plan, a partitioning scheme you've actually tested, and an honest read on whether the vest and strict pull-ups belong in your version this year. The workout will still be hard. It's supposed to be. It doesn't have to be reckless, and it shouldn't be rushed just to post a fast time.

If you want to build a warm-up or a scaled companion piece around whatever equipment you have, the WOD Builder can put one together in a few clicks. And logging your result with a free account means next year you're not guessing whether you got faster. You'll know.
